title: TensorRT Edge-LLM Completes the MLPerf Edge Agentic Benchmark 6.4x Faster on Jetson AGX Thor | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA's TensorRT Edge-LLM ran Qwen3.6-27B on a single Jetson AGX Thor and finished the MLPerf Inference v6.1 Edge Agentic workload (1,007 turns) in 24m36s at 52.33 tokens/sec, 6.4x faster than the llama.cpp reference. The gains come from Blackwell-only NVFP4 weight/activation quantization, FP8 KV cache, ~96% hot-cache prompt token reuse across agent turns, and tree-based multi-token prediction worth ~40% extra decode performance on function-calling workloads.

insights.claim: NVIDIA's TensorRT Edge-LLM ran Qwen3.6-27B on a single Jetson AGX Thor Developer Kit and completed all 1,007 turns of the MLPerf Inference v6.1 Edge Agentic performance workload in 24 minutes and 36 seconds, 6.4x faster than the llama.cpp reference run's 2 hours and 37 minutes.
insights.speaker: Luxiao Zheng
insights.so_what: A 6.4x margin over the most common open-source edge LLM runtime is the core commercial argument for paying for NVIDIA's proprietary inference stack on edge silicon.
insights.quote: The system achieved 52.33 tokens per second and completed all 1,007 turns of the performance workload in 24 minutes and 36 seconds, 6.4x faster than the llama.cpp reference submission of 2 hours and 37 minutes.
insights.locator: MLPerf Edge Agentic benchmark results on Jetson AGX Thor

insights.claim: The submission posted 52.33 output tokens per second, a 247.12 ms median time to first token, a 14.68 ms median time per output token, and 87.94% overall BFCL accuracy in SingleStream mode on one device with 128 GB unified memory at MAXN power mode.
insights.speaker: Luxiao Zheng
insights.so_what: Concrete latency and accuracy numbers let buyers judge whether a 27B-parameter agent is deployable on a single edge module rather than in the cloud.
insights.quote: Output throughput52.33 tokens per secondMedian time to first token247.12 msMedian time per output token14.68 msBFCL overall accuracy87.94%
insights.locator: Table 1, MLPerf v6.1 NVIDIA Edge Agentic submission result summary

insights.claim: The comparison baseline is not a tuned competitor but the MLCommons-published llama.cpp reference run using Q4_K_M quantization on the same Jetson AGX Thor hardware, meaning the 6.4x gap measures software stack difference on identical NVIDIA silicon rather than a cross-vendor chip comparison.
insights.speaker: Luxiao Zheng
insights.so_what: The headline speedup is a software moat claim, not a silicon claim, so it is defensible only as long as open-source runtimes lag on NVFP4 and speculative decoding.
insights.quote: The MLCommons Edge Agentic example also publishes a llama.cpp reference run on Jetson AGX Thor, which uses Qwen3.6-27B with Q4_K_M quantization and completes in 2 hours and 37 minutes.
insights.locator: MLPerf Edge Agentic benchmark results on Jetson AGX Thor

themes.theme: Agentic workloads redefine edge inference requirements

insights.claim: AI agents are migrating from cloud data centers into vehicles, robots, and other edge devices, where the model must select tools, evaluate results, and keep reasoning inside a growing conversation rather than answering a single prompt.
insights.speaker: Luxiao Zheng
insights.so_what: If agentic inference genuinely moves to the edge, it opens a device-side silicon TAM distinct from datacenter GPU demand.
insights.quote: AI agents are moving from cloud data centers to vehicles, robots, and other edge devices.
insights.locator: Introduction

insights.claim: Edge agentic inference imposes three simultaneous constraints that a chatbot does not: fast token generation, efficient processing of long shared histories, and valid tool calls, all within a limited power and memory envelope.
insights.speaker: Luxiao Zheng
insights.so_what: This three-way constraint is the design spec competitors must hit; single-metric benchmarks like raw tokens/sec understate the difficulty.
insights.quote: The model must generate tokens quickly, process long shared histories efficiently, and produce valid tool calls within a limited power and memory envelope.
insights.locator: Introduction

insights.claim: The MLPerf Edge Agentic performance phase replays recorded software-engineering agent trajectories across 20 conversations and 1,007 generated turns, with input length growing to roughly 23.5K tokens, making long-context processing a first-class part of the measurement.
insights.speaker: Luxiao Zheng
insights.so_what: The benchmark's design bakes in prefix-reuse advantage, favoring runtimes with sophisticated KV cache management over simple decode-optimized ones.
insights.quote: The workload contains 20 conversations and 1,007 generated turns. Input length grows across turns and reaches approximately 23.5K tokens
insights.locator: How MLPerf measures end-to-end agentic AI performance

insights.claim: The accuracy phase uses Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard v4 prompts restricted to single-turn with reasoning off, an explicit tradeoff to balance accuracy fidelity against evaluation time on edge devices.
insights.speaker: Luxiao Zheng
insights.so_what: The accuracy gate is deliberately narrowed, so 87.94% BFCL is not evidence of multi-turn reasoning quality under quantization.
insights.quote: The accuracy phase uses Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL) v4 prompts with single-turn only and reasoning off to balance accuracy and evaluation time on edge devices.
insights.locator: How MLPerf measures end-to-end agentic AI performance

insights.claim: An MLPerf co-author chairs the MLCommons Agentic Edge Inference task force that defined the first industry standard benchmark for AI agent workloads on edge devices, so NVIDIA staff helped shape the benchmark on which NVIDIA submits.
insights.speaker: Luxiao Zheng
insights.so_what: Benchmark authorship overlap is a standing reason to discount vendor-reported MLPerf leadership claims when comparing across vendors.
insights.quote: He chairs the Agentic Edge Inference task force in MLPerf Inference at MLCommons, which defined the first industry standard benchmark for AI agent workloads on edge devices.
insights.locator: About Palanivel Guruva reddiar

themes.theme: NVFP4 quantization and the memory-bandwidth bottleneck

insights.claim: Low-batch LLM decoding on edge platforms is heavily bounded by DRAM bandwidth, so shrinking both weights and activations reduces kernel memory footprint and directly boosts decoding performance.
insights.speaker: Luxiao Zheng
insights.so_what: Bandwidth, not FLOPs, is the binding constraint at the edge, which is why numeric format support is the decisive architectural feature.
insights.quote: Low-batch LLM decoding on edge platforms is known to be heavily bounded by DRAM bandwidth.
insights.locator: Using NVFP4 quantization to accelerate Qwen3.6-27B inference

insights.claim: The submitted model uses NVFP4, a 4-bit floating-point format supported by the Blackwell GPU inside Jetson AGX Thor, for weights and activations including the language-model head, plus FP8 for the KV cache.
insights.speaker: Luxiao Zheng
insights.so_what: NVFP4 is hardware-gated to Blackwell, so the format becomes a generational upgrade lever and a switching cost for anyone on non-Blackwell parts.
insights.quote: NVFP4 is a 4-bit floating-point format supported by the NVIDIA Blackwell GPU in Jetson AGX Thor.
insights.locator: Using NVFP4 quantization to accelerate Qwen3.6-27B inference

insights.claim: Compressing the model frees more of the 128 GB unified memory for long context, speculative decoding state, and the application workloads sharing the device, so quantization buys headroom for the rest of the robot or vehicle stack rather than just speed.
insights.speaker: Luxiao Zheng
insights.so_what: On an embedded device the LLM competes with perception and control stacks for memory, making footprint reduction a systems-integration argument, not just a latency one.
insights.quote: The smaller model representation also leaves more of the 128 GB unified memory available for the long context, speculative decoding state, and application workloads.
insights.locator: Using NVFP4 quantization to accelerate Qwen3.6-27B inference

insights.claim: Deployment friction is reduced by publishing a pre-calibrated Qwen3.6-27B NVFP4 checkpoint, so a team can either download it or run post-training quantization once on any development system before deploying.
insights.speaker: Luxiao Zheng
insights.so_what: Shipping calibrated checkpoints lowers the skill barrier and pulls more third-party developers into the NVIDIA edge toolchain.
insights.quote: A deployment team can use a published quantized checkpoint or perform post-training quantization once on any development system before deploying the model.
insights.locator: Using NVFP4 quantization to accelerate Qwen3.6-27B inference

themes.theme: KV cache reuse across agent turns

insights.claim: Because each agent request repeats most of the preceding conversation plus a new response or tool result, a runtime without prefix reuse must re-prefill the shared history every turn at a cost that grows with conversation length.
insights.speaker: Luxiao Zheng
insights.so_what: Repeated prefill is the hidden dominant cost of agentic workloads and the main lever separating naive runtimes from optimized ones.
insights.quote: Without reuse, the model must prefill the shared history again on every turn. The cost increases as the conversation grows.
insights.locator: Reusing KV cache across agent turns

insights.claim: On this workload roughly 96% of prompt tokens were served from hot cache, with the runtime prefilling only about 0.5M of the 13.6M total prompt tokens across all turns.
insights.speaker: Luxiao Zheng
insights.so_what: A 27x reduction in prefill work is the single largest contributor to the end-to-end speedup and is largely orthogonal to raw hardware performance.
insights.quote: On this workload, ~96% of the prompt tokens are served with hot cache. The runtime only prefills ~0.5M of the total 13.6M prompt tokens across the turns.
insights.locator: Reusing KV cache across agent turns

insights.claim: Because Qwen3.6 uses a hybrid model architecture, the runtime must restore recurrent state and partial KV-page state in addition to cached attention KV pages, a correctness requirement that simple prefix-caching implementations do not handle.
insights.speaker: Luxiao Zheng
insights.so_what: Hybrid attention-recurrent models raise the engineering bar for cache reuse, widening the gap between vendor runtimes and community ones.
insights.quote: Qwen3.6 uses a hybrid model architecture, so the runtime also restores the recurrent state and partial KV-page state required to continue execution correctly.
insights.locator: Reusing KV cache across agent turns

insights.claim: Cache reuse and multi-token prediction are presented as complementary rather than overlapping optimizations, because cache reuse cuts cost before generation begins while MTP cuts the number of target-model steps during generation.
insights.speaker: Luxiao Zheng
insights.so_what: A mental model for evaluating any inference stack: prefill-side and decode-side optimizations multiply, so single-technique comparisons mislead.
insights.quote: cache reuse reduces the cost before generation begins, while MTP reduces the number of target-model steps during generation.
insights.locator: Reusing KV cache across agent turns

themes.theme: Tree-based multi-token prediction and function calling

insights.claim: Tree-based multi-token prediction organizes high-probability draft candidates into a tree that the target model verifies in one forward pass, advancing generation by several tokens when multiple candidates are accepted, versus linear MTP which keeps only a single predicted continuation.
insights.speaker: Luxiao Zheng
insights.so_what: Tree speculation converts branch uncertainty into parallel verification, a general technique any inference vendor will have to match.
insights.quote: Instead of keeping only one predicted continuation, the runtime organizes high-probability candidates into a tree.
insights.locator: Using tree-based multi-token prediction to accelerate LLM inference

insights.claim: With 8 draft steps, top-2 candidates at each drafting depth, and a 16-node verification tree, tree-based MTP delivered roughly 40% additional decoding performance over a linear MTP with 3 draft steps on this workload.
insights.speaker: Luxiao Zheng
insights.so_what: A ~40% decode gain from a configuration change alone shows how much headroom is left in speculative decoding tuning rather than in hardware.
insights.quote: Compared with a linear MTP with 3 draft steps, tree-based MTP could achieve an additional ~40% decoding performance gain for this workload.
insights.locator: Using tree-based multi-token prediction to accelerate LLM inference

insights.claim: Function-calling workloads are unusually favorable to tree verification because tool names, JSON syntax, and common argument structures are highly predictable while multiple branches preserve likely alternatives for individual argument values.
insights.speaker: Luxiao Zheng
insights.so_what: Speculative-decoding speedups are workload-dependent, so agentic tool-calling benchmarks will flatter this technique relative to open-ended chat.
insights.quote: Tree-based verification is useful for function calling because tool names, JSON syntax, and common argument structures are often predictable
insights.locator: Using tree-based multi-token prediction to accelerate LLM inference

insights.claim: Recent frontier models now ship official multi-token-prediction weights trained alongside the main model, meaning speculative decoding is becoming a model-release deliverable rather than a runtime-side hack.
insights.speaker: Luxiao Zheng
insights.so_what: If MTP heads ship with open weights by default, the speculative-decoding advantage shifts from model vendors to whoever writes the best verification runtime.
insights.quote: Recent models typically have official MTP weights trained and shipped together with the main model.
insights.locator: Using tree-based multi-token prediction to accelerate LLM inference

insights.claim: The full submission is reproducible from a public branch, release/0.9.1-mlpinf of NVIDIA/TensorRT-Edge-LLM, which ships model export settings, TensorRT engine build commands, server configuration, and MLPerf client configuration.
insights.speaker: Luxiao Zheng
insights.so_what: Publishing a runnable branch converts a marketing benchmark into an adoption funnel and makes the claim falsifiable by third parties.
insights.quote: The implementation used for this submission is available on the TensorRT Edge-LLM release/0.9.1-mlpinf branch.
insights.locator: How to run the MLPerf Edge Agentic benchmark

insights.claim: The server is exposed as an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so the MLPerf harness and downstream applications can target NVIDIA's edge runtime without rewriting client code.
insights.speaker: Luxiao Zheng
insights.so_what: API compatibility lowers migration cost onto NVIDIA's runtime while keeping migration off it equally cheap, so the lock-in is in the kernels, not the interface.
insights.quote: Launch the OpenAI-compatible TensorRT Edge-LLM server.
insights.locator: How to run the MLPerf Edge Agentic benchmark

insights.claim: The benchmark configuration pins temperature 0, seed 42, reasoning disabled, and concurrency 1, a determinism-first setup that measures single-stream latency rather than throughput under multi-user load.
insights.speaker: Luxiao Zheng
insights.so_what: Concurrency 1 means these numbers say nothing about how the device behaves serving multiple agents at once, the realistic robotics case.
insights.quote: The supplied configuration runs the performance and accuracy phases with temperature 0, seed 42, reasoning disabled, and concurrency 1.
insights.locator: How to run the MLPerf Edge Agentic benchmark

insights.claim: NVIDIA pairs this edge submission with a companion datacenter result for Vera Rubin NVL72 in the same MLPerf Inference v6.1 round, presenting a single inference software stack spanning edge and server scale.
insights.speaker: Luxiao Zheng
insights.so_what: The edge-to-datacenter continuity story is the strategic payload: one toolchain across form factors raises the cost of adopting a competing edge accelerator.
insights.quote: For server-scale Vera Rubin performance, see NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 Delivers Leading Performance in MLPerf Inference v6.1 Debut.
